branding.metaDescription: QuakeStudio — an educational earthquake response simulator. Not a structural safety assessment.
branding.disclaimerShort: Educational simulation using simplified assumptions. Not a structural safety assessment.
branding.disclaimerLong: This is a learning tool, not a safety check. QuakeStudio uses a simplified model with stated assumptions. Its results say nothing about whether a real building is safe.

copy.topbar.saveTooltip: Saved in this browser. Export from the dialog to move runs elsewhere.

copy.topbar.assumptionsTooltip: What the model assumes, and what its results do not tell you.

copy.results.heading: Results
copy.results.peakDisplacementHelp: The furthest any floor moved sideways, measured from the ground beneath it.
copy.results.maxStoryDriftHelp: The biggest gap between one floor and the floor below it, as a percentage of floor height.
copy.results.naturalPeriodHelp: How long the building takes to sway back and forth once, at its natural rhythm.
copy.results.compareHelpOn: {count} buildings felt the same earthquake. Pick one on the left to edit it.
copy.results.compareHelpOff: Adds a second, third or fourth configuration and runs them all under one earthquake.
copy.results.displacementNote: is sideways movement from the ground, in millimetres. Each line is one floor.
copy.results.driftNote: is the difference between one floor’s peak and the floor below’s, as a percentage of floor height. The difference is taken between the peaks, not instant by instant.
copy.results.periodNote: is the time for one full sway at the building’s natural rhythm. A longer period is not by itself better or worse.
copy.playback.note: Motion is drawn {exaggeration}× larger so millimetres are visible. The numbers themselves are not exaggerated — but they are still the model’s output, not a validated result.
copy.playback.reducedMotion: Reduced-motion is on, so playback starts paused at half speed.
copy.desktop.heading: QuakeStudio is built for a laptop or desktop
copy.desktop.body: The workspace needs three columns side by side. On a smaller screen the panels would be too narrow to read.

glossary.definition: How far a floor moves sideways, measured relative to the ground beneath it.
How much one floor moves compared with the floor below it. A bigger gap means more strain between the two.
Drift as a percentage of floor height, so tall and short floors can be compared fairly.
How quickly the shaking dies away after it stops. More damping means the building settles sooner.
The time it takes the building to sway back and forth once. Taller buildings have a longer period.
The building’s own natural rhythm — it always sways at this pace unless something forces it faster.
Peak Ground Acceleration — how strong the shaking is at its most intense moment.
How hard the building resists being pushed sideways. Stiffer buildings sway less.
How heavy the building is. Heavier buildings respond more slowly.
Rigid corners join the beams and columns, so the frame bends rather than folding inward.
Diagonal braces stiffen the frame, so it resists sideways movement much more strongly.
When the shaking rhythm matches the building’s own rhythm, it builds up much more than you would expect.
Real movement is tiny, so the 3D view multiplies it so you can see it. The numbers stay true.
The movement of the ground itself, which the building has to follow.
A number that makes random shaking repeatable, so the same shake comes back every time.

steps.title: Set up your building
steps.body: Pick a template, then set how many floors it has, how big each one is, what it is made of, and whether the frame is braced. Every one of those changes how the building answers a shake.

steps.title: Give each floor a use
steps.body: Choose what each floor is for — office, home, parking or storage — or type your own dead and live loads. The use sets how much live load is counted, which changes the building’s weight and how it sways. These are teaching defaults, not a design check.

steps.title: Shake it
steps.body: Press play to run the earthquake. The movement you see is drawn about {exaggeration} times larger than it really is, so the sway is easy to follow — but the numbers are never scaled. That setting only changes the drawing.

steps.title: Read the numbers
steps.body: Peak displacement, max story drift and natural period. Colour on the building shows how far each floor moved compared to its own height. These come from a teaching model, not from a safety check.

steps.title: Compare two buildings
steps.body: Turn on compare to add a second building and watch both react to the same earthquake. Useful for asking what actually makes a building handle shaking better.

welcome.title: Welcome to QuakeStudio
welcome.description: Build a simple building, shake it, and watch how it sways.
welcome.acknowledgement: I understand that results are for learning only.
welcome.footer: Every coefficient in this tool is a placeholder waiting for review by a structural engineer. The Assumptions button in the top bar lists them all.

steps.title: Build
steps.body: Pick a template or change the floors, size, material and frame type.

steps.title: Shake
steps.body: Choose how strong and how fast the ground moves, then press play.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Add a second building and see how the sway and the numbers differ.
